findings.message: `proposalEvent` finds a pinned history line by rebuilding the whole page. `historyOf` reads only the newest 100 audit rows, the newest 100 phase-change events and Time's newest 100 rows. So a line that still exists but has aged out of that window gives `null`, the same answer as a line that is gone or one the viewer may not see. In chat's resolver, a pin whose `proposalId` arg is present and whose `of()` returns null keeps its old label. The pin then shows stale text instead of saying it can't be read. Fix: look the line up directly by its kind and id (`audit:<seq>` → `core.audit_event` where seq = …, `event:<id>`, `task:<id>`, and `time:<seq>` through Time's slot with a single-line lookup). Keep 'not visible' apart from 'not found'.
findings.scenario: A proposal has 101 or more audited edits and task closes. Someone pinned its 'Created' line (`audit:12`) earlier. Calling `get_proposal_event({proposalId, line:'audit:12'})` returns null although the audit row exists, so the pin can never be relabelled or read.

findings.message: `limit 100` runs in SQL before the `mayFix` visibility filter. When the proposal has more than 100 newer time rows from other people, an entry's owner gets no lines of their own: the page shows 'no time lines', when really they were never read. This file is new in the diff (the rule moved here from Delivery). Fix: filter by visibility first (owner = viewer, or the viewer approves the project) and then apply the limit, or page per viewer.
findings.scenario: Team members log 120 entries on CON-014 after Nimal's single 2 h entry. Nimal opens CON-014 and sees no line for their own 2 h, though `mayFix` allows it.

findings.message: `setProposalHours` is a `defineService`, so it opens its own transaction on a second pool connection while the handler's transaction still holds the advisory locks and its `onceForEvent` claim. Sorted locks keep the ordering safe. But each refresh holds two connections, and if the handler's transaction fails after the service commits, the retry writes a second audit row for the same event. Consider passing the totals back so the write happens after the handler's transaction, or document the two-connection need for small pools (such as Hyperdrive).
findings.scenario: The service commits, then the handler transaction's commit fails. The outbox retries and `delivery.proposal.hours` gets two audit rows for one event.

findings.message: The AC28 test sets the module-global slot with `setProvided([...stub])` and clears it only on the last line. If any assertion fails before that, the stub leaks into every later test in the worker and changes their history output. Put the reset in a `finally` or an `afterEach`.
findings.scenario: The `lines(maya)` expectation fails, `setProvided([])` never runs, and later history assertions in the file see stub time lines.

findings.message: `pinOf.event` sets the resolved id to the proposal's id, not the line's id. The registry's pin check therefore treats every line of a proposal as the same record: a pin with a wrong `line` but the right `proposalId` still passes. Key the pin on proposalId plus line, for example `id: "line"` or a composite, so the check proves it reached that exact line.
findings.scenario: Pin args {proposalId: P, line: 'audit:12'}, and the registry compares the resolved id against P only. Swapping in another line of P passes the check unnoticed.

findings.message: `provided()` returns an empty slot both when no installed module fills it and when `setProvided` was never called in this process. Only `apps/web/lib/registry.ts` sets it. Any entry point that renders or serves proposal detail without loading the registry would silently show 'no time logged' instead of 'unknown'. `hasModule` already tells these apart with null. Do the same here: start with null and fail or flag when a slot is read before it is set.
findings.scenario: A process loads Delivery's tools without apps/web/lib/registry (a script or test harness) and calls get_proposal. Time lines are left out with nothing to show that the slot was never set.

findings.message: `setProposalHours` is exported from contracts.ts, and the doc says it runs under a job context with no grant to anyone. Nothing enforces 'Time is the only caller': any module that builds a `contextFor.job` can overwrite every proposal's hours in a project. Restrict it to the Time job's actor, for example by checking `ctx.actor` is `job:time.proposal-hours`.
findings.scenario: Another module calls setProposalHours(contextFor.job(t, 'x'), {projectIds:[P], totals:{}}). Every proposal in P is set to 0 h.
